item.title: “Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What…
item.description:
“Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of a skeleton, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse. These ten perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.57

item.title: “Monks, if one does not intend, does not plan but still has a tendency towards something, that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness.…
item.description:
“Monks, if one does not intend, does not plan but still has a tendency towards something, that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is an establishment of consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. With name-and-form as condition, the six sense-bases … such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.39
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Form, sound, taste, smell, touch — All these things Are desirable, delightful, agreeable As long as they exist. The world with its devas Regards them…
item.description:
“Form, sound, taste, smell, touch —
All these things
Are desirable, delightful, agreeable
As long as they exist.

The world with its devas
Regards them as delightful,
But when they cease,
Then they are seen as suffering.

The noble ones see as happiness
The destruction of identity.
This is completely opposite
To what the whole world sees.

What others call happiness,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as happiness.

The good have open eyes, they see, they have light —
Apart from the noble ones,
Who is worthy of perfect enlightenment?
By that right knowledge of the path,
They attain Nibbāna, free from defilements.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 3.12
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Good sirs, what is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning and relinquishing of…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. Good sirs, what is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the cessation of suffering, namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 9 – Sammādiṭṭhisutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms. Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s body thrown in the charnel ground, one, two, or…
item.description:
“Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms. Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s body thrown in the charnel ground, one, two, or three days dead – bloated, discolored, festering. What do you think, monks? Has the former charm and beauty disappeared and peril become evident?”
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, whatever is greed — that is unwholesome. Whatever a person does bodily, verbally, or mentally with greed — that is unwholesome. When a person…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is greed — that is unwholesome. Whatever a person does bodily, verbally, or mentally with greed — that is unwholesome. When a person with greed, overcome by greed, with mind uncontrolled, makes another suffer — by killing, binding, confiscation, abuse, or expulsion — thinking ‘I am strong, I have power’ — that is unwholesome. Thus, many evil, unwholesome states arise in him born of greed, originating from greed, produced by greed.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.69
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, when the child grows up and his faculties become mature, he enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure fully: forms cognizable by the eye…
item.description:
“Monks, when the child grows up and his faculties become mature, he enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure fully: forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. When he sees a form with the eye, he lusts after a pleasing form and dislikes a displeasing form. He dwells with mindfulness not established on the body, with a limited mind. He does not know as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder. Thus, in relation to the body, whichever feeling arises — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and clings to it. Because he delights, welcomes, and clings, delight in sensual pleasure arises. With delight in sensual pleasure, there is clinging. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 38 – Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with…
item.description:
“Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, there is knowledge: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.15
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Sunāga: “Skilled in the mind’s signs, Knowing the taste of seclusion, Meditating, mindful, careful, He attains the non-worldly happiness.”
item.description:
Elder Sunāga:
“Skilled in the mind’s signs,
Knowing the taste of seclusion,
Meditating, mindful, careful,
He attains the non-worldly happiness.”

From: Theragāthā 1.85

item.title: “As rain seeps into a house with a faulty roof, So lust seeps into an undeveloped mind.” “As rain does not seep into a house…
item.description:
“As rain seeps into a house with a faulty roof,
So lust seeps into an undeveloped mind.”

“As rain does not seep into a house with a good roof,
So lust does not seep into a well-developed mind.”

From: Dhammapada 1-20
